# Beat analysis: tempo ambiguity and downbeats

The comparison target is strict musical tempo, beat/downbeat timing, continuity,
manual correction effort and measured throughput/RAM against independently
checked annotations. A pinned Traktor Pro 4 build is a comparison candidate;
perfect automatic variable grids are not assumed. See [BEAT_BENCHMARK.md](BEAT_BENCHMARK.md)
for the versioned exporter/evaluator, decoder timelines and an untouched holdout.

The existing Queen Mary tracker identifies a clean 174 BPM synthetic pulse
as 87 BPM at 44.1, 48 and 96 kHz. This is a reproducible metrical-level
ambiguity, including when alternate pulses are quieter. The change adds an
audio-evidence check for constant-tempo analysis, after Queen Mary tracking
and before the existing beat-grid construction.

## Implemented behavior

The tracker additionally computes an onset envelope from a two-stage 200 Hz
low-pass signal. This supplies evidence for additional low-frequency pulses
without treating high-frequency subdivisions alone as a reason to double
the tempo. It does not isolate a drum stem.

For a coherent constant-tempo result, the refiner compares tempo multiples
1/2, 2/3, 1, 3/2 and 2 in a 40–240 BPM search interval. Pulse precision
penalizes predicted beats without supporting onsets; strength-weighted onset
recall penalizes onsets missed by the grid. Their harmonic mean ranks the
candidates. Peak strength is square-root compressed to retain quieter beats.

A change requires at least 16 detected onsets, 80% pulse support, a score
of at least 0.85, an improvement of at least 0.08 over the original tempo,
and a lead of at least 0.04 over the next candidate. These are conservative
engineering thresholds, not probabilities or calibrated confidence values.
The original result is retained when evidence is insufficient or ambiguous.
Variable-tempo analysis bypasses this constant-tempo correction entirely.

The refiner also compares the supplied grid phase with the best supported
phase at the same tempo. It can correct a half-beat displacement when the
same conservative support and improvement thresholds are met. Queen Mary
previously did not classify bar downbeats in Mixxx. The optional native
downbeat integration is described below. In Auto mode its refinement is applied
only after the unrefined result passes the constant-grid fit check below.

The Queen Mary analysis subversion changes so the existing reanalysis
preference can distinguish old and new results. BPM locks and the user's
choice not to reanalyze existing grids remain effective. Existing library
grids are not migrated automatically. Request a fresh analysis of unlocked
tracks to use the changed detector.

## Beat This! integration

Beat This! is now an optional analysis provider in Preferences > Beat
Detection. Queen Mary remains the default. Select **Beat This! (local
model)**, choose the Python interpreter and local checkpoint, and leave the
SHA-256 field at its default for the official `final0` model. Apply the
settings and request reanalysis of unlocked tracks. Existing grids and BPM
locks follow the existing reanalysis preferences.

The integration runs the official Python inference implementation in an
external process on the analysis worker, using CPU PyTorch and `dbn=False`.
Audio is downmixed to mono and streamed into a temporary float32 file;
no audio is uploaded. Mixxx does not download models or install Python
packages during analysis. One persistent process per analysis thread imports
Python and loads the model once, then accepts sequential jobs. Startup has a
60-second limit and each job a 10-minute limit. Cancellation kills the active
worker; the next job can start a fresh process. The analyzer commits results only after successful
validation; a failed run leaves any grid still present on the track untouched.

The process uses protocol 2 UTF-8 JSON lines: optional `startup_progress` messages,
a verified `ready` handshake, job IDs, progress, a nested version-1 result, and
recoverable or fatal errors. Startup progress covers checkpoint verification,
Python imports and model loading; it does not extend the startup deadline.
Custom Models also reports completion of the first model when that backend
has no incremental progress callback, so the display does not remain at the
50% decoding boundary during the second model's startup. Parallel analysis
and persistent worker reuse are unchanged. Requests
are limited to 64 KiB and responses to 8 MiB. Replies with the wrong ID, invalid
positions, malformed progress or a protocol mismatch are rejected. Crashes,
timeouts and fatal errors discard the session; ordinary invalid jobs can leave
it reusable. Runtime/script/checkpoint identity changes cause a restart. The
checkpoint is hashed before loading and its file identity is checked for every
job. Each analysis thread owns its process, so jobs do not cross thread boundaries.
The existing batch scheduler releases its threads after completion, and worker
shutdown is explicit at thread exit. Reuse adds no new analysis threads.

The one-shot CLI remains supported for installation checks and controlled
comparisons. `MIXXX_BEAT_THIS_ONESHOT=1` selects it in the C++ backend; `--timings`
adds measurements to direct CLI output. Neither mode changes the official
prediction algorithm, the 22,050 Hz model resampling, CPU thread counts or the
checkpoint. Real cross-rate tests compare exact one-shot and warm results at
22,050, 48,000 and 44,100 Hz.

For an interactive user-local Linux build/install, including the Python
environment, checkpoint and automatic path configuration, see
[LINUX_INSTALL.md](LINUX_INSTALL.md) and run `python3 tools/install-linux.py`.
It offers compilation alone or installation with a desktop starter.

The worker requires Beat This! 1.1.0. A manual Linux CPU setup is:

```sh
python3 -m venv /path/to/beat-this-env
/path/to/beat-this-env/bin/python -m pip install --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu 'torch==2.5.1+cpu' 'torchaudio==2.5.1+cpu'
/path/to/beat-this-env/bin/python -m pip install -r tools/requirements-beat-this.txt
curl -fL https://cloud.cp.jku.at/public.php/dav/files/7ik4RrBKTS273gp/final0.ckpt -o /path/to/final0.ckpt
sha256sum /path/to/final0.ckpt
```

Expected `final0` SHA-256:
`8c328b45f59d8dd3dff219253ff6a8d6482be57d0133a29140e2febbf8eb8331`.
The worker verifies this fingerprint before loading the checkpoint. Other
checkpoints require their own independently verified fingerprint. Models
and Python dependencies are not bundled into the Mixxx binary. The Linux
installer sets them up separately in user-owned directories.

In this cloud environment the interpreter is
`/workspace/mixxx-beat-this-env/bin/python` and the checkpoint is
`/workspace/mixxx-env/beat-this-final0.ckpt`. These are outside the checkout.
The official main model is approximately 78 MB. Its download and inference
have both succeeded in this environment.

Downbeats are kept separately from beat timing. They are projected onto the
resulting Mixxx grid, stored in additive protobuf fields, restored when the
track is loaded, and shown as wider beat markers by both waveform rendering
paths. A constant grid uses its first retained downbeat as its anchor. Grid
translations move the downbeats too; manual tempo scaling or BPM changes
clear the labels because the beat interpretation has changed. This adds
explicit downbeat markings, not automatic bar-level synchronization or meter
editing. Old Mixxx versions can read the beat data but discard the new
fields if they save it again.

## Custom Models

**Custom Models** is an additional entry beside Queen Mary, SoundTouch and
Beat This! in the analyzer selector. It contains only two model assignments:
**Model for Constant** and **Model for Variable**. Both offer Queen Mary and
Beat This!, with Queen Mary/Beat This! as the initial pair. Beat This! uses
the existing shared Python/checkpoint/SHA-256 settings. SoundTouch remains
available as a separate legacy BPM-only provider.

The existing Auto, Constant and Variable controls remain in use. Explicit
Constant/Variable uses only its assigned analyzer. Auto first evaluates the
Variable analyzer's full-track beats with the clock-fit check below. With
usable percussive audio evidence, it also finalizes the Constant analyzer
and compares both assigned results against the audio. This validates the
actual Constant result rather than assuming it has the Variable model's
tempo. The selected result still comes from its assigned model. Both
analyzers must initialize successfully. Failures do not silently substitute
the other analyzer's output or replace an existing grid.

When both assignments are identical, Auto runs that analyzer once and
compares its two grid representations. Standalone analyzers use the same
audio validation and phase correction. Model assignments, backend versions and
the shared model fingerprint enter the analysis cache identity. A choice
used only by Variable does not invalidate an explicit Constant result, and
vice versa. The existing reanalysis preference and BPM locks still apply.
Changing assignments affects subsequent analyses; existing grids are not
silently converted. Applying preferences saves the assignments immediately.
The Linux installer now preserves an existing provider selection, including
Custom Models, when refreshing Python/model paths.

## Optional Queen Mary downbeats

**Mark Queen Mary downbeats (4/4 estimate)** enables the `DownBeat` algorithm
already included in the bundled QM DSP library. It needs no neural model
or Python process. It compares spectral differences between beat segments
and estimates the four-beat bar phase; it is not Beat This!'s classifier.
It is disabled by default and independent of the Custom Models assignments.

Audio is downmixed in contiguous 1,024-frame blocks and decimated 16 times.
Beat positions are converted to that block coordinate system after the
existing Queen Mary tempo/phase refinement. The implementation requires at
least 16 in-range beats and at least three spectral comparisons per bar
phase. Non-finite, effectively zero or ambiguous phase scores are omitted;
the strongest mean must exceed the runner-up by at least 10%. These are
engineering abstention thresholds, not calibrated accuracy/confidence.

Accepted labels remain on detected beats, enter the existing downbeat
storage and waveform marker paths, and follow the same editing rules as
Beat This! labels. The assumption is fixed four beats per bar: changing
meters, ambiguous arrangements and an already misplaced/incorrect beatgrid
can yield absent or incorrect labels. This addition does not resolve the
previously reported Gnosis beat-phase error. The synthetic spectral-change
regression checks a 4/4 signal, not annotated real-song downbeat accuracy.

## Auto, Constant and Variable

Preferences > Beat Detection now offers three grid modes. The track analysis
menu also offers overrides for individual tracks without changing the global
preference.

- **Auto** fits a clock over the full track before assessing sustained
  timing drift. A search within 0.8% of the original constant candidate
  maximizes circular phase coherence on a half-beat lattice. This handles
  temporary offbeat/subdivision mistakes without doubling the reported BPM.
  The search uses at most 1,024 sampled predictions and three refinement
  passes. No Python dependency or second model run is added.
  Phase estimates in 32-beat windows separate smooth drift from isolated
  tracker phase steps. Short tracks use smaller windows, with at least eight
  beats per window and 32 predictions overall. At least four reliable windows,
  80% reliable windows and 0.65 global coherence are required. Reliable
  windows have at least 0.7 circular coherence; these are engineering cutoffs,
  not confidence probabilities.
  An isolated phase increment exceeding 40 ms or 8% of a beat, whichever
  is larger, can be treated as a nuisance phase change. Consecutive
  increments in the same direction are retained as drift; short gaps of
  incoherent tracking can also separate nuisance phase steps. At most two
  such steps, or one per eight reliable windows for longer tracks, are
  accepted. After removing a linear timing trend, the 5th-to-95th-percentile
  phase span must fit within 50 ms or 10% of a beat, whichever is larger.
  The first and last two reliable windows are also checked separately against
  a 40 ms/8% limit, so sustained end drift cannot simply be trimmed away.
  Window beat-interval averages additionally guard against real half/double
  or 2:3 tempo changes being mistaken for offbeat slips: the central 20–80%
  period range and the start/end period ratio must stay within a factor of 1.25.
  Otherwise Auto selects Variable.
- **Constant** forces a single-tempo grid. For providers that preserve raw
  beat positions, including Beat This!, the fitted clock replaces coarse
  region-based tempo rounding. Where at least four stable 64-beat regressions
  are available, their 10%-trimmed mean supplies the tempo. Each regression
  must stay within 40 ms of its local straight grid and within 0.8% of the
  fitted clock. Without identified tracker phase steps, the local estimate
  must also stay within 25 ms cumulative timing difference over the entire
  track; otherwise the global clock is retained. This prevents repeated
  local timing biases from accumulating into a drifting constant grid.
  A circular full-beat mean supplies the grid phase. Native
  Queen Mary explicit Constant analysis keeps its existing construction.
- **Variable** preserves Beat This! beat positions directly, including tempo
  changes. It bypasses the Queen Mary-oriented region smoothing previously
  applied to every provider. Downbeats remain attached to those positions.

Dense variable beat maps also need a stable representative BPM. A histogram
of single intervals can report 130.43 BPM for a quantized 133.15 BPM pulse,
or 136.36 BPM for 138 BPM. For maps with at least 16 tempo markers and fewer
than four beats per marker on average, the BPM summary now uses 16-beat
neighborhood estimates. Whole-BPM buckets collect small variations, and a
time-weighted mean within the dominant bucket supplies the reported value
to two decimal places. This changes neither beat timing nor the local
beat-position-based tempo. Sparse maps retain their existing calculation.

Auto is the default for a fresh configuration. Existing constant/variable
preferences are migrated to the corresponding explicit mode. Auto is a
timing heuristic, not a measurement of model confidence or proof of intended
musical tempo. A genuine abrupt phase edit and a tracker phase error can
look identical in beat timestamps. Explicit Variable remains available
when such edits must be represented. Low-coherence predictions can still
cause a physically constant song to use a variable grid.

The conservative clock-fit follow-up used `auto:2` and Beat This! backend
identity `3`. The subsequent audio-validation pass uses `auto:3`,
`audio_grid_evidence:3` and Custom Models backend `2`. The neural checkpoint
and prediction algorithm are unchanged; worker transport uses protocol 2. Request reanalysis of unlocked tracks to replace
old results; BPM locks and reanalysis preferences still apply.

Fast analysis is available only in Constant mode. Auto and Variable analyze
the full track even if an old configuration still has fast analysis enabled.
Model identity, backend version and Auto mode are recorded in the analysis
subversion, so changing these can trigger reanalysis when that preference is
enabled. BPM locks and the existing reanalysis preference remain effective.

Applying beat-detection preferences now saves them to disk immediately.
Refreshing the dialog blocks widget change signals so programmatic updates
cannot be mistaken for user selections. A reproduced display bug also showed
Queen Mary instead of the saved provider while BPM detection was disabled:
the disabled dialog returned before populating its selections. It now shows
the saved provider and grid mode in that state too. This does not establish
that every reported intermittent reset had that cause. Opening an older Mixxx
build with the same profile can still overwrite settings it does not support.

## Audio validation and phase correction

The next round adds audio evidence rather than tuning a threshold for each
recording. `BeatGridEvidence` accumulates an auxiliary mono waveform at about
1 kHz during decoding. The exact fractional rate is retained, including at
44.1 kHz. Offline forward/backward low-pass filters at 85, 150 and 300 Hz
avoid imposing a causal filter delay. Smoothed energy rises identify attacks;
their time reference lies between the steep rise and its following crest.
Strengths are normalized against an eight-second local envelope, with a
track-relative energy floor and 70 ms peak suppression. Silence supplies
no positive evidence. This is onset evidence, not drum-stem separation.

For each candidate, Gaussian timing tolerances of 12 and 25 ms measure
supported predicted pulses and strength-weighted onset recall. Their
harmonic mean balances pulse precision and onset coverage; comparisons
between different pulse densities need the additional guard below.
Scores use the low and broad channels; the intermediate channel corroborates
small timing corrections. A fourth full-band RMS envelope retains snare and
hi-hat transients that disappear when averaging the waveform before low-pass
filtering. Half-beat changes also need corroboration from this envelope and
2.5 times the other phase's full-band pulse precision. When snares still
support the original phase, louder offbeat kicks must not move the grid;
ambiguous windows provide no phase-change evidence. This is a conservative
engineering cutoff, not an estimate of the probability of a phase edit.
The comparison retains full-band support at the unchanged grid as well as
at the bass-optimized fine offset, so that searching for kicks cannot erase
the snare evidence that should veto a half-beat shift.
Phase searches consider the supplied beat family
and its half-beat alternative, with fine offsets limited to 75 ms or 15%
of a beat, whichever is smaller. Candidate clocks are ranked at their
attainable phase; translating a grid requires additional evidence.

Auto favors Constant unless Variable improves one of these two scores by
more than 0.08, or a sustained phase edit requires a map. A usable candidate
can also replace an unsupported one. With insufficient evidence, the earlier
clock-only decision remains the fallback. These scores and cutoffs are
engineering heuristics, not calibrated probabilities or benchmark accuracy.

When the Variable candidate is sparser than Constant and its 90th-percentile
beat interval exceeds 1.25 times its 10th percentile, compare pulse precision
against the same number of beat opportunities. Keep strength-weighted onset
recall unchanged, and recompute the two-band F1 scores. This prevents a
tracker alternating among half-time and 2:3 levels from improving precision
simply by omitting harder beat lines. A steady half-tempo candidate keeps
its original score; there is no general preference for doubling BPM.
When full-band evidence is available, a normalized Variable candidate must
also improve full-band pulse support; following sparse kicks alone cannot
override a stable snare/hi-hat clock.
The phase search still optimizes the original F1 score, so this normalization
is a conservative ranking heuristic rather than an optimal joint search.

Sparse percussion can support both fewer hits at unchanged tempo and a real
metrical tempo change. This rule favors a supported Constant clock when the
alternative changes pulse density; abrupt half/double-tempo changes can
therefore remain ambiguous. Full-band corroboration does not identify the
intended musical meter. Explicit Variable remains available.

Fine translations must improve support on both halves of the recording.
A translation larger than 10 ms is rejected when it reduces full-band F1 by
more than 0.02 on both halves and the original support is at least 0.2 in each.
In that case retain the original phase, including abstaining from the small
subframe fallback. This prevents the crest of a soft bass body from pulling
an already aligned percussive attack later. These are engineering guards,
not calibrated probabilities or a fixed early offset.
A more conservative correction of at most 10 ms can compensate for the
50 Hz model's timestamp quantization when two of the three frequency
channels agree on both halves. Global half-beat changes require a stronger
score gain and corroboration from low and broad attacks. Existing downbeat
labels move with the beat lines; no new bar or meter classifier is added.

For longer phase mistakes, a two-state dynamic program evaluates Same/Half
beat families in 16-second windows, with a switching penalty of 0.08. A
regional change additionally needs 128 beats of active, corroborating
evidence. Uncertain windows and silence cannot extend a short fill into a
supported structural edit. Whole-track half shifts still need whole-track
corroboration. Supported boundaries are refined against individual attacks
within the surrounding windows instead of being snapped to 16-second edges.
When needed, Auto stores the corrected phase regions as a variable map even
if the tempo elsewhere is steady. The corrected map is evaluated before
comparing candidate quality. Explicit Constant remains a single-tempo grid;
explicit Variable bypasses this audio refinement and preserves the selected
provider's existing variable-grid behavior.

With different model assignments, ambiguous Auto tracks may now require
both backends to finalize. Constant=Beat This!, Variable=Queen Mary therefore
can run one neural inference even when the final choice is Variable. This
adds work relative to the former Queen-Mary-only Variable route. Identical
assignments still use one inference. There are no new Python requirements,
checkpoint downloads, per-song rules or model-training steps.

Torch uses two intra-operation threads and one inter-operation thread.
Warm jobs reuse imports, checkpoint verification and the model; preprocessing
and inference still run for every recording. Stage measurements cover decoder,
PCM writing, startup/import/model load, preprocessing, inference, postprocessing,
grid refinement and in-memory track attachment. The `storage` stage does not
measure deferred library database writes. Parent/worker timings overlap and
must not be added indiscriminately. Worker RSS is explicitly its process-lifetime
high-water mark, not total Mixxx RAM or a per-job delta. See the benchmark guide
for measured controls and remaining corpus/comparison limitations.

Set `MIXXX_TEST_PHASE_GRID_TRACK_DIRECTORY` to the local fixture directory
containing the nine named mono `.f32` files and official `*-baseline.json`
worker outputs. It may also contain the previous six recordings plus HMC
and Gnosis. `PhaseAndMetricalAudioRegression` runs native Queen Mary,
replays the cached neural predictions, checks routing and the noted phase
directions, and writes grid reports and before/after beat times outside
the repository. With the Python/model environment variables set, the full
`UploadedCustomModelsChooseConservativeGridTypes` test analyzes every fixture
through actual model calls, annotation, progress, cache metadata and grid
serialization. No original audio or private prediction fixtures are committed.

Synthetic ground-truth tests separately exercise fine timing, chunk sizes,
sample rates, long 44.1 kHz clock accuracy, half-beat labels, offbeat hi-hats,
short fills, sustained phase edits, non-window-aligned edit boundaries,
metrical switches, drifting Constant candidates and genuine tempo changes.

## Syncopated breakbeat regression recordings

The third supplied set exposes a distinction between rhythmic arrangement
changes and changes in the underlying clock. Bass-only half-phase evidence
incorrectly rejected the Constant candidates for Splash and Apollo Two.
In Code Red, Queen Mary's sparser, metrically switching grid gained precision
by skipping pulses. Full-band corroboration and the guarded common-density
comparison address those mechanisms without recording-specific rules.

With Constant=Beat This!, Variable=Queen Mary and Auto, the supplied recordings
are checked as Constant at approximately 163.55 BPM (Splash – Babylon),
157.40 BPM (Apollo Two – Atlantis, L.T.J. Bukem Remix), and 170.28 BPM
(Code Red – Conquering Lion). These whole-track estimates agree with the
user's independently supplied reference BPMs; the complete analysis test
checks agreement within 0.02 BPM. The previous 17 fixtures
remain included, especially G-Man, Bazetoya, HMC and the true half-beat edits.

Synthetic breakbeats vary kicks independently of snares and hats; controls
move the entire pattern, introduce smooth tempo drift, or supply a genuine
steady half-tempo pulse. Original audio and prediction files stay outside
the repository. No new Python libraries, checkpoints or training are needed.
Add `splash.f32`, `apollo.f32`, `code-red.f32` and their official
`*-baseline.json` worker outputs to `MIXXX_TEST_PHASE_GRID_TRACK_DIRECTORY`
to include these recordings in both the cached and complete-model tests.

## Soft-bass timing regression

For Eurogroove – Move Your Body Part 1, the user verified Constant 135.93 BPM
and an approximate 40 ms advance relative to the previous grid. Native libmad
analysis produces 135.92741 BPM. The previous audio refiner moved its already
aligned model clock approximately 46.32 ms later toward the bass crest; the
new full-band contradiction guard retains the original clock. The observed
change agrees with the user correction to approximately 6 ms, without applying
a recording-specific offset. Earlier useful Jeff Mills/Ellen Allien timing
corrections and all previous grid-type references remain regression cases.

The user's correction and independent waveform/onset diagnostics support this
regression, but do not constitute complete manual beat/downbeat annotations.
The benchmark leaves those quality fields unavailable. MP3 decoder-origin
mapping is a separate issue: libmad and FFmpeg gapless decodes differ by about
25.06 ms for this file, so a cross-decoder comparison must record its timeline.

## Conservative Auto regression recordings

The six supplied recordings were decoded in full as mono float32 at 44.1 kHz.
The original Auto check classified all six as Variable, using both the cached
`final0` predictions and native Queen Mary Variable predictions. In the user's
Custom Models setup, Queen Mary's 70 BPM result for Donkey Rhubarb therefore
remained selected instead of the roughly 140 BPM Beat This! result.

The regression tests check both providers' Auto decisions and the complete
Custom Models path with Constant=Beat This!, Variable=Queen Mary. Slow,
coherent curvature in Bazetoya remains distinguishable from the temporary
Queen Mary phase displacement in Black Circles and its return to the grid.
No track names, target BPM values or recording-specific exceptions enter
the production algorithm. Music and full model predictions remain outside
the repository.

The Black Circles regression also checks the median grid distance at the
beginning and end against the model's beat positions. Synthetic checks cover
short tracks at 44.1/48 kHz, quantization, temporary/permanent tracker phase
steps, offbeat slips, small returning timing excursions, smooth tempo drift,
sustained end drift and 120-to-240/80 BPM changes. A repeated 20 ms local
timing-bias case guards against roughly 0.1 BPM tempo error and up to 215 ms

Set `MIXXX_TEST_AUTO_GRID_TRACK_DIRECTORY` to a local directory containing
`acid`, `aphex`, `aural`, `bazetoya`, `black` and `mike-ink` mono `.f32` files
and their `*-baseline.json` official-worker outputs. The beat-clock regression
also runs native Queen Mary over these files. With
`MIXXX_TEST_BEAT_THIS_PYTHON` and `MIXXX_TEST_BEAT_THIS_MODEL` set as above,

checks grid type, the reported Aphex/Black Circles tempos, progress, downbeat

These user-labelled examples are a targeted regression set. They establish
neither general accuracy nor parity with Traktor Pro 4: no paired Traktor
outputs or independent annotated music benchmark were available for this
comparison. Constant/Variable routing accuracy, strict tempo accuracy,
beat phase and bar/downbeat accuracy are separate evaluation targets.

## Analysis progress and supplied logs

Model inference still runs after audio decoding. Previously decoding took
the progress display to 95%, then the entire Python/model job ran without
updates. Beat This! jobs now reserve 0–50% for decoding and 50–95% for model
preparation and inference; final result storage completes the job. The worker
reports each completed model window through job-identified JSON messages in
persistent mode and the legacy stderr protocol in one-shot mode.
This is stage progress, not an estimate of remaining wall-clock time. The
official preprocessing, inference and postprocessing remain in use.

Both supplied tracks were decoded and evaluated in full with `final0`:

| Track | Audio length | Beat predictions | Initial worker time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| HMC – Body Mechanics | 560.07 s | 1,243 | 28.16 s |
| Parallel 9 – Gnosis | 465.17 s | 1,062 | 27.14 s |

The instrumented worker returned exactly the same beat and downbeat arrays
as the previous worker for both files. It emitted 25 and 22 progress updates,
respectively. These timings include Python startup and model loading on this
CPU environment; they are not a general speed guarantee.

The uploaded-track regression verifies every saved and restored variable
beat against the model within one audio sample at 44.1 kHz. The previous
variable-grid smoothing displaced predictions by up to 24.44 ms for HMC and
38.38 ms for Gnosis. Auto selects Variable for both files; their new
representative variable-grid BPM values are 133.04 and 137.94, respectively.
These are summaries of changing/local predictions, not annotated ground truth.

Queen Mary's measured median distance to the Beat This! predictions remains
59.80 ms for HMC and 189.77 ms for Gnosis with the conservative refiner.
The added phase correction does not resolve these original-track cases.
It passes the synthetic half-beat-offset regression; that is not evidence
of correct bar/downbeat classification on these recordings.

The supplied logs contain 124 expected M4A/MP4 container-alias warnings and
ten empty-temporary-filename warnings. The valid M4A-to-MP4 alias no longer
produces a warning, and Beat This! initialization avoids removing an unnamed
temporary file. ICC profile, OpenGL teardown, audio-device and database
warnings have different sources and are not diagnosed as neural inference
failures by this work.

## Verification and limits

The Queen Mary audio regression matrix covers 80, 96, 120, 140 and 174 BPM at
44.1, 48 and 96 kHz, with uniform, alternating and every-third-beat accents:
45 synthetic audio scenarios. It checks tempo and beat phase (15 ms maximum
error). Additional checks exercise 1/2 and 2/3 input hypotheses,
high-frequency subdivisions, noise, changing tempo, silence, reused
analyzers, input chunking, fast-analysis boundaries, stored analysis
versions and protected grids.

Beat This! checks cover result validation, checkpoint fingerprints,
downbeat serialization for constant and variable grids, and grid edits.
The storage test includes ten successive round trips at 174 BPM, where a
beat spans a fractional number of audio frames.
The optional real-model C++ test runs the complete path through
`AnalyzerBeats`, the Python process, grid construction and serialization.
Enable it by setting `MIXXX_TEST_BEAT_THIS_PYTHON` and
`MIXXX_TEST_BEAT_THIS_MODEL` to the interpreter and official `final0` paths.
Without these variables this test is explicitly skipped. Python protocol
checks run with `python3 -m unittest tools/test_beat_this_worker.py`.

The follow-up adds real-model validation of a 76-second track changing from
120 to 144 BPM, Auto/Constant/Variable selection, legacy-setting migration,
immediate preference persistence, programmatic dialog refresh, progress
callbacks, and quantized-BPM summaries at 44.1 and 48 kHz.
The optional uploaded-track case uses `MIXXX_TEST_BEAT_THIS_TRACK_DIRECTORY`
with local `hmc.f32`, `gnosis.f32` mono float32 files at 44.1 kHz and their
`*-baseline.json` model results. Original music files are not included in
the repository.

Final validation in this environment: the Debug build succeeded; all 1,351
active CTest cases passed, including the real-model integration tests,
the 21 complete Custom Models analyses and the supplied-track regressions.
The 38 existing disabled cases remained disabled; no active test was skipped.
All 62 installer/worker/benchmark Python tests, Black, Flake8 and formatting checks
for the changed C++ files passed.
Mixxx also initialized its database, loaded the LateNight skin, opened
virtual audio output and entered its event loop in the headless startup
check. This does not validate hardware audio or GPU rendering.

These synthetic checks demonstrate integration and regressions, not
accuracy on a representative music collection. A 4/4 pulse with subdivisions
can support several metrical interpretations. The neural model also makes
mistakes; it does not guarantee the intended tempo or musical “1” for every
track. The supplied regression cases are now covered, but a broader annotated
music collection is still needed to assess generalization and genre regressions.

Direct `final0` worker runs on two generated 24-second drum fixtures returned
mean beat rates of 119.90 and 173.91 BPM for targets of 120 and 174 BPM.
The 120 BPM fixture produced mixed two- and four-beat downbeat intervals;
its bar interpretation is therefore not established as correct. The 120 BPM
run, including Python startup and model loading, took 6.66 seconds with
approximately 510 MiB peak resident memory while a build was also running.
This historical single measurement is not a throughput benchmark. It used
the previous per-track Python process and model-loading path; warm reuse is
now described above and measured separately in the benchmark guide.

This follow-up is developed on `feat/beat-this-variable-tempo`. The previous
implementation remains on `feat/beat-this-analysis` at `a6db4edf42`.

## Research consulted

- [Beat This!](https://github.com/CPJKU/beat_this), Foscarin, Schlüter and
  Widmer, ISMIR 2024: [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21658). This
  transformer predicts beats and downbeats jointly, with optional DBN
  postprocessing. The official repository documents Python/PyTorch
  inference, approximately 78 MB main models and 8.1 MB small models; code
  and published weights are MIT licensed according to its current README.
  This integration uses its official preprocessing and inference. Supported
  release packaging and real-music runtime/accuracy evaluation remain open.
- [BeatNet](https://github.com/mjhydri/BeatNet), ISMIR 2021:
  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.03576). Its CRNN and particle filter
  jointly track beat, downbeat, tempo and meter in causal modes; the
  documented offline mode instead uses DBN decoding. This is a useful
  alternative when streaming latency matters; it is not integrated here.

For a follow-up benchmark, report strict tempo accuracy separately from
half/double and 2:3/3:2 errors; accepting metrical alternatives as correct
would hide the reported DJ problem. Measure beat timing and downbeat/bar
accuracy separately, include ambiguous and variable-tempo material, and
record per-genre regressions plus CPU and memory. Listening and testing on
an actual DJ setup remain required before contribution submission.
